message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Feasibility Study: Robotic Palletising on Lines 1 and 2
Operations Engineering, Kestrel Foods, Wrexley Plant, February 2026

1. Purpose
This study assesses whether to replace manual palletising at the end of packing Lines 1 and 2 with two robotic palletising cells, and recommends a course of action to the Plant Investment Board.

2. Current operation
Lines 1 and 2 pack savoury snacks into cases, which are stacked onto pallets by hand at the end of each line. Each line has two palletising operators per shift, and the lines run two shifts a day (06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00), five days a week. That is eight operator posts in total. At a fully loaded cost of £36,500 per operator per year, manual palletising costs £292,000 a year.

Palletising is the most physically demanding task on site. Operators lift around 4,000 cases per shift, and the task accounts for most of our manual-handling injuries.

Under the site plan agreed by the Board in December 2025, Lines 1 and 2 will move to a single day shift from January 2027, as volume consolidates onto the new high-speed Line 5.

3. The proposed solution
Each cell consists of a four-axis robot, a layer-forming conveyor, a pallet dispenser, safety guarding and a stretch-wrapper. One operator per shift would supervise both cells, handle pallet changes and clear faults.

Vendor trial
The preferred vendor ran a three-day trial in January using our actual cases and pallet patterns.

Table 1. Vendor trial results, 12-14 January 2026
Case type | Share of Line 1 and 2 volume | Peak rate (cases/min) | Sustained rate over 8 hours (cases/min)
14 kg catering case | 60% | 13 | 10.5
8 kg retail case | 40% | 16 | 14.0

Our lines run at up to 12 cases per minute. The trial confirmed that the cell sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types, comfortably above our line rate, so the cell will not become a bottleneck.

4. Safety benefit
Line 3 has had an automated case packer and palletiser since 2023. In 2025 it recorded 4 manual-handling injuries, compared with 11 across Lines 1 and 2. Automation clearly reduces injuries, and we expect robotic palletising to cut manual-handling injuries on Lines 1 and 2 by a similar proportion. For context, Line 3 runs the lighter 6 kg multipack cases and operates on a single shift.

5. Costs and savings
Table 2. Financial summary
Item | Amount
Capital: two cells, installed, including guarding and conveyors | £620,000
Annual maintenance contract (two cells) | £36,000
Remaining supervision: one operator per shift, two shifts | £73,000 per year
Current manual palletising cost | £292,000 per year
Net annual saving (£292,000 - £73,000 - £36,000) | £183,000
Simple payback (£620,000 / £183,000) | 3.4 years

The Plant Investment Board's hurdle for automation projects is a payback of four years or less, so the project meets the hurdle with a margin. The three operators displaced on each shift would be offered redeployment to Line 5, which is currently recruiting.

6. Implementation
The vendor quotes a 16-week lead time. Installation would take place during the planned two-week August shutdown, with a further two weeks of commissioning at reduced line speed. We would train two engineering technicians on robot maintenance as part of the contract.

7. Risks
Changeovers to new case sizes require reprogramming, which the vendor will provide for the first year. Pallet quality varies between suppliers, and poor pallets cause faults in automated dispensing; we will tighten our pallet specification before go-live.

8. Recommendation
Robotic palletising on Lines 1 and 2 is technically proven on our own products, removes our most injurious manual task and pays back in 3.4 years, within the Board's four-year hurdle. We recommend the Board approve capital of £620,000 for installation in the August 2026 shutdown.
</document>
response:
# Review: Robotic Palletising Feasibility Study (Lines 1 and 2)

The study is clearly written and its arithmetic is internally correct. However, it omits a change the Board has already approved, and it misreads its own trial data. With those corrected, the project **does not meet the four-year payback hurdle**, and the cell may not keep up with the line on the main product. The recommendation is not supported as it stands.

## Critical issues

### 1. The savings ignore the move to a single shift (Sections 2 and 5)

Section 2 says Lines 1 and 2 move to a single day shift from January 2027. Section 5 still costs everything on two shifts. The cells would go live around September 2026, so only about four months would run at the two-shift baseline.

Re-based on one shift from January 2027:

| Item | Study (2 shifts) | Corrected (1 shift) |
|---|---|---|
| Current manual cost | £292,000 (8 posts) | £146,000 (4 posts) |
| Remaining supervision | £73,000 (2 posts) | £36,500 (1 post) |
| Maintenance | £36,000 | £36,000 |
| **Net annual saving** | **£183,000** | **£73,500** |
| **Simple payback** | **3.4 years** | **≈8.4 years** |

The few months of two-shift savings in late 2026 shorten this only slightly. The project fails the hurdle by a wide margin.

Half of the claimed saving comes from second-shift posts that the consolidation removes anyway. Crediting them to the robot double-counts a saving the Board has already approved. This also undercuts the redeployment point: those operators would move to Line 5 regardless.

### 2. The trial does not show the cell keeps up with the line (Section 3)

The text says the cell "sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types." Table 1 shows otherwise:

- **14 kg catering case: 10.5 cases/min sustained**, which is below the 12 cases/min line rate. This case is 60% of volume.
- Only the 8 kg retail case reaches 14 cases/min.

On catering cases, the cell would be the bottleneck. Two things need resolving:
- Is "up to 12 cases/min" a peak or the typical rate? For example, 4,000 cases per shift averages about 8.3/min if that figure is per line. Buffering might absorb short peaks, but this has to be shown, not assumed.
- Does the vendor have a faster configuration for the heavy case, and at what extra cost?

Note that the 14 kg case is both the main injury driver and the case the robot handles worst.

### 3. The safety comparison doesn't support the conclusion (Section 4)

The study concedes that Line 3 runs lighter cases (6 kg) on a single shift, but draws its conclusion anyway. On exposure:

- Line 3: 4 injuries over 1 line × 1 shift = **4 per line-shift**
- Lines 1 and 2: 11 injuries over 2 lines × 2 shifts = **2.75 per line-shift**

Adjusted for exposure, the automated line has the *higher* rate. Other weaknesses:
- There is no before/after baseline for Line 3.
- Line 3 also automated case packing, so the effect of the palletiser can't be isolated.
- We don't know which tasks caused Line 3's injuries.

The safety case may still be strong. Palletising 4,000 heavy cases a shift is an obvious risk. But it should rest on Lines 1 and 2's own injury records by task, plus a manual-handling risk assessment, not on this comparison.

## Other gaps

- **Uncosted items:**
  - lost output during two weeks of reduced-speed commissioning
  - technician training time
  - reprogramming after year one
  - work to tighten the pallet specification, and any increase in pallet cost
  - project management and contingency
- **Staffing assumption:** can one operator supervise two cells on separate lines, including pallet changes, fault clearing and wrapper film changes? Fault frequency from the trial would help answer this.
- **Line life:** volume is consolidating onto Line 5. What is the expected remaining life and volume of Lines 1 and 2? A payback of over eight years on lines being run down is a serious concern.
- **Analysis depth:** there is no sensitivity analysis, NPV, or risk-adjusted view, and no alternatives are considered.
- **Timing:** the study targets the August 2026 shutdown. If it is being reviewed now (November 2026), that date has passed and the plan needs re-dating.

## Suggested way forward

1. Re-base the financials on the single-shift operation from January 2027, including all one-off costs.
2. Get a vendor commitment on sustained rate for the 14 kg case at the actual line rate, or a costed upgrade.
3. Rebuild the safety case from Lines 1 and 2's own injury data and risk assessment.
4. Compare lower-cost options, which may achieve most of the safety benefit within the hurdle:
   - vacuum lift-assists
   - a single cell dedicated to the 14 kg case
   - a shared cell
5. If the safety benefit is the real driver, present the project as a safety investment, judged against safety criteria, rather than forcing it through the payback hurdle.

**Bottom line:** the study should not go to the Board in its current form. Once the approved shift change is included, payback is roughly 8.4 years against a four-year hurdle. The throughput and safety claims also need to be restated to match the evidence.
